p01.text: Before dawn on March 8 the Israeli Air Force bombed Iran’s oil facilities for the first time in the war. Four people were killed. Black smoke from the storage tanks spread over the capital. The sun came up and it did not get light. There were fears of fuel shortages, of poisoned water and soil, of damage to people’s lungs. The war’s targets were moving from military sites to the country’s livelihood.

p02.text: The same day U.S. and Israeli forces said they had hit the Revolutionary Guards’ Aerospace Force headquarters and 50 ammunition depots. CENTCOM announced a seventh American service member killed by Iranian attacks. In Kuwait City a drone set a high-rise on fire, and two Kuwaiti officers died on duty. A third U.S. aircraft carrier was on its way to the Middle East.

p03.text: On March 9 the Assembly of Experts named Mojtaba Khamenei, the dead leader’s second son, as the new Supreme Leader. He had never held public office. The same day the Safavid palaces of Chehel Sotoun and Ali Qapu in Isfahan were badly damaged. An explosion near Manama, Bahrain, injured 32 people, and the state oil company BAPCO declared force majeure.

p04.text: On March 10 the U.S. military said it had struck several Iranian minelayers trying to mine the strait. No one could say whether mines were already in the water. In Tehran an intersection on the Resalat Highway was hit, with heavy civilian casualties. The UAE’s Ruwais refinery shut down. The U.N. refugee agency said about 700,000 people had fled their homes in Lebanon.

p05.text: On March 11 Israeli drones struck checkpoints inside Tehran, killing at least ten people. One of them was an eleven-year-old boy. Just out of the strait, the bulk carrier Mayuree Naree was hit by two missiles, and two more merchant ships were damaged. Marine insurance had jumped four- to sixfold in a week. Oman’s Salalah port stopped operations.

p06.text: The sun came up. It did not get light. Maryam, a nurse, came off the night shift and stood at the ward window. The sky over Tehran was the color of ink. The emergency room had been full since four. Not people hurt by shrapnel. People coughing. Children with asthma, old people with weak lungs. By midnight half the oxygen tanks were empty. Today she learned breath. The sound a person makes when they cannot breathe.

p07.text: In the hospital dorm, seven-year-old Nariman had her chin on the windowsill. “Maman, it’s morning. Why is it night?” “Because oil is burning. A very big oil tank. It’ll take a few days.” “So it’s night for a few days?” Nariman drew a sun with her finger on the fogged glass. One circle, eight lines. A bomb hurts only the people it hits. Smoke chooses everyone who breathes.

p08.text: Dr. Leila Shirazi looked from one screen to the other. On the left, Tehran. Black smoke cut across the city. On the edge of the band sat the Evin district, where her aunt lived. Nine days without a phone line. On the right, Fordow. The signal held at yesterday’s level. Sam Farrell brought two coffees. “Word from the liaison office. Tel Aviv asked about your Fordow report. Raw data and all.”

p09.text: “But look at that. They didn’t hit the mountain. They hit the oil.” Instead of breaking what could not be broken, they chose to choke the country’s breath. The grammar of the war had changed overnight. The report spoke of a mountain, and the decision chose oil. “It’s a choice.” Leila zoomed all the way in on Evin. The satellite would not show her roses. Target lists name buildings, never the people downwind.

p10.text: Before dawn on March 9, Capt. Marcus Webb watched from the bridge as the map grew. Ten days ago only two countries had been colored in. Now the color had spread. Lebanon, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Oman. The sea off Cyprus, the skies over Turkey. Twenty-five years in the Navy, and no manual covered a war that spread this far in ten days.

p11.text: Sarah Callahan’s place was empty. Before she left she gave him a page torn from her notebook. The Bahrain bureau’s number, and one line below it. The days your hands are quiet scare me most. He kept it in his breast pocket. Marine insurance had jumped sixfold in a week. On a map a war spreads as color. At sea it comes as distance. The distance at which you cannot help.

p12.text: The name was announced. Col. Darius Sepahvand stood in front of the same television as eight days before. The Islamic Republic’s third Supreme Leader: Mojtaba Khamenei. The dead leader’s second son. For eight days he had lived as a body without a head. Turn the radar on, and a missile came within the hour. Turn it off, and he was blind. He had lost eleven men. He had saved nineteen.

p13.text: Now there was a head. He found he felt no relief. This country was built by driving out a king. It shed blood to end the son inheriting the father’s seat. The new chain of command’s first message was short. All units hold present positions. The strait stays closed. “Acknowledge receipt. Send only that.” The body had a new head. Where was that head looking?

p14.text: When the sirens went off, Sarah Callahan had been in Bahrain thirty hours. Concrete walls, fluorescent lights, folding chairs. Beside her sat a uniform with the Korean flag on the shoulder. “Lt. Kim Junho, South Korean Navy.” A dull thud in the distance. Dust drifted down from the ceiling. His hand curled once on his knee and opened again. Sarah saw it, and pretended she hadn’t.

p15.text: “What does a liaison officer do?” “I count ships. Korean ships and Korean sailors stuck in the Gulf. How many days of water and food they have left.” A captain had told him yesterday: Lieutenant, we’re not targets, we’re more like hostages. “Aren’t you scared?” “I am. But when I start calling out the ships’ names in the morning, I’m all right. If you have something to count, you hold on.” Sarah memorized it.

p16.text: At 11:40 p.m. on March 10, Lt. Kim Junho was writing to his father. His father was a quiet man. So was the son. Between two quiet men, writing came easier than talk. Dear Father. I have not fired a shot yet. For someone like me this war is screens and numbers. But there are people behind the screens. I try not to forget that the numbers are people.

p17.text: The ships whose names I know are out on that water. The captains ask when they can leave. I didn’t know “I don’t know” could be so hard to say. Every day I learn again what you told me the day I was commissioned: lose the power to think, and you’re no longer a soldier. He wrote it by hand. The tremor of the letters, the smudge of the ink. War is lived in letters in envelopes.

p18.text: Soraya Tahir was hauling a broken door. In six days it would be Chaharshanbe Suri, the night when every alley lights a fire and people jump over it. “Still doing it this year? Plenty of fire’s coming down from the sky.” “That’s why we’re doing it. That’s their fire, and this is ours.” At the end of the alley stood a checkpoint. Two of the four there were boys. Their rifles were too long for their bodies.

p19.text: One of them, cracking sunflower seeds, looked at her. The way a kid looks at a big sister carrying a door. She could not hate him. That made her angry. “Hey. Don’t stand there. Go home.” That night word came that checkpoints elsewhere in the city had been hit. At the end of her alley the sandbags were still there. No one was. Only sunflower seed shells on the ground.

p20.text: Professor Azad Moradi’s notebook was full. He took out his lecture notes, the lecture he had meant to give on the morning of February 28: Kant’s Perpetual Peace. The backs were blank. No paper fit a war better. He wrote. The new leader’s name has been announced. A son. After forty-seven years we have come back to the same place. Only this time, a turban instead of a crown.

p21.text: History was not a circle. It was a spiral, passing the same place at a slightly different height each time. And on the spiral, spring came every year. Into the gunfire, into the black smoke. Spring did not ask permission. At that hour in Seoul, Kang Yujin fed hundreds of dots stalled in the Gulf into her model. The machine gave an answer. What could the people inside those dots be sure of tomorrow?

cover_threads.text: The Report Said Mountain. They Chose Oil.
